# Final Review Proposal
**Producer:** agent:claude/claude-opus-4-6

## Summary

Reviewed the shrimp ingestion→assimilation→excretion→feces→respiration routing implementation across shrimp.rs, budget.rs, process.rs, presets.rs, and the test suite. The core mass conservation logic is mathematically correct: consumed N and C are partitioned through feces (→detritus), excretion (N→TAN, C→DOC), respiration (C→DIC, N→TAN, O2 consumed), and retention (→reserve_g) with exact round-trip conservation verified by unit tests and 7-day closed-system integration tests. The O2-limited respiration scaling correctly diverts unrespired material to reserve while maintaining stoichiometric coupling. Death routing properly transfers both body mass and proportional reserve to detritus. Budget accounting includes reserve_g as a tracked component for both N and C. All 8 shrimp_feeding_pathway tests pass plus the full test suite. Three amendments proposed: (1) the v3→v4 migration should seed reserve_g for existing populations instead of defaulting to 0, (2) alkalinity should be adjusted when TAN is produced by excretion/respiration to prevent systematic pH drift, and (3) a minimal maintenance drain on reserve_g would prevent unbounded accumulation over long runs.

## Amendments

1. The v3→v4 save migration for `reserve_g` should seed the reserve proportionally to the existing shrimp population instead of defaulting to 0.0. When an old save with an established colony (e.g. 30 adults, 20 juveniles) is loaded, `reserve_g = 0.0` causes all hatching (`fund_hatched_clutch_biomass`) and juvenile maturation (`fund_live_shrimp_biomass`) to fail until enough feeding cycles accumulate reserve. The migration function `migrate_v3_to_v4` should compute a reasonable initial reserve — e.g. `reserve_g = shrimp_biomass_g(adults, juveniles) * LIVE_BIOMASS_ORGANIC_FRACTION_G_PER_G` — so established populations don't experience a transient reproduction/growth block on upgrade.
   Rationale: This is a correctness issue for save/load compatibility. A no-op migration silently degrades an established simulation: existing berried females will fail to hatch, and juveniles won't mature, until ~7+ feeding days accumulate enough reserve. Users loading old saves will see unexplained population stagnation. The fix is a one-line computation in the migration function.
2. Add an alkalinity adjustment when TAN is produced by shrimp excretion and respiration in `route_consumed_food`. When amino acids are catabolized, each mole of NH3/NH4+ released increases alkalinity by approximately 1 meq. The current code adds TAN to `ammonia_total_mg_n_total` but does not adjust `alkalinity_meq_total`. At the excretion+respiration rates in this model (excr_frac=0.10, resp_frac=0.70 of assimilated N), omitting this coupling will cause pH to drift lower than it should over time because the DIC increase from respiration suppresses pH without the counterbalancing alkalinity increase from ammonia release. Add: `state.water.alkalinity_meq_total += (excreted_n_mg + respired_n_mg) / 14.007` (converting mg N to meq NH3).
   Rationale: This affects pH accuracy. The carbonate system is recalculated via `refresh_carbonate_state` after feeding, but without the alkalinity contribution from TAN production, pH will systematically underestimate by an amount proportional to feeding rate. In a tank with 10+ shrimp and moderate feeding, this could amount to 0.1-0.3 pH units of drift over weeks — enough to affect condition and molt stress calculations downstream. The fix is a single addition line and the stoichiometry is well-established.
3. Phase 1 `reserve_g` has no maintenance drain and will grow without bound over multi-month or multi-year simulation runs. While the code comment at shrimp.rs:245-248 acknowledges this, the unbounded accumulation means the N+C budget will increasingly shift into the reserve pool. Consider adding a minimal daily maintenance drain (e.g. `reserve_g *= (1.0 - maintenance_fraction)` with maintenance_fraction as a named parameter, default ~0.01/day) that routes the drained mass to TAN+DIC via the same respiration pathway. This keeps reserve bounded, adds metabolic realism, and provides a natural hook for the later condition/molt work.
   Rationale: Without any drain, a 10-shrimp tank feeding daily will accumulate ~0.01-0.02g of reserve per day. After 6 months of simulation, reserve_g could reach several grams — exceeding the total shrimp body mass. This distorts the mass budget (large fraction of N/C trapped in reserve) and makes the later Phase 2 reserve/condition work harder because it inherits unrealistic initial conditions. A simple exponential drain is cheap and prevents this drift.
